analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for seniors and applies payroll taxes to all high wages.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2024, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would do two things. First, it would change how annual Social Security cost-of-living increases are calculated, using an inflation index that tracks what people 62 and older actually buy — which typically rises faster than the index used now, meaning bigger yearly increases for retirees, disabled workers, and survivors. Second, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages above the annual taxable cap, phasing that in from 2025 through 2030, so the highest earners pay into the program on all of their wages instead of stopping at the cap. High earners would receive a small amount of extra benefit credit for those earnings, but far less than the extra tax they would pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries — retirees, disabled workers, and surviving spouses — would get larger annual cost-of-living increases, since an index built on the spending of households headed by people 62 and older (which is weighted more toward health care and housing) generally rises faster than the general wage-earner index used today [S2]. The bill explicitly protects the poorest beneficiaries: any increase would not count as income for Supplemental Security Income or Medicaid eligibility, so seniors would not lose other benefits because their Social Security check went up [S2]. The program as a whole would gain revenue, because tax collected on wages above the cap flows into the same trust funds that pay everyone's benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Cost-of-living adjustments would be calculated using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers that reflects the spending patterns of people 62 and older, which typically produces larger annual increases than the current index.

The bill applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages and self-employment income above the annual contribution and benefit base, phasing in from 14 percent of wages above the cap in 2025 to fully covering them after 2030.
New benefit factors of 3 percent and 0.25 percent would apply to earnings above the cap, giving high earners a modest benefit credit for the extra taxes they pay.
Any benefit increase from the new inflation index could not reduce or eliminate a recipient's eligibility for Supplemental Security Income or Medicaid.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people whose earnings exceed the annual taxable maximum (about $168,600 in 2024) would pay Social Security payroll tax on their wages above that line, phasing in over six years starting in 2025. For the self-employed, that means the full self-employment tax rate applies to income above the cap. Their extra benefit credit — 3 percent on the first slice of high earnings and 0.25 percent beyond it — is far smaller than what the standard benefit formula pays on earnings below the cap, so high earners would pay substantially more in tax than they would get back in benefits. Employers would also owe the matching half of the payroll tax on their high-paid employees' wages above the cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: The bill breaks the traditional link between what high earners pay in and what they receive: they would pay tax on all wages above the cap but earn benefits at only a 3 percent or 0.25 percent factor, so most of the extra tax would never come back to them as benefits — a fairness objection supporters of the current earnings cap raise in good faith.

Employers would owe a matching payroll tax on wages above the cap, and self-employed people above the cap would pay the full rate on all their income, which critics of payroll tax increases argue can reduce hiring or wages for high-salaried workers and add compliance complexity for small-business owners.

Switching to a senior-specific inflation index raises costs permanently and compounds over a lifetime of benefits; opponents of benefit expansions generally argue the program should first address its projected financing gap rather than add spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people the bill targets, the benefits are real and direct: larger annual increases that better track what seniors actually spend on medical care and housing, plus a guarantee that the poorest beneficiaries would not lose SSI or Medicaid because their check grew. The cost falls on a narrow group — earners above the taxable maximum — who would pay materially more in tax than they receive back in benefits, since the bill deliberately credits them with only a small slice of benefit for the extra contributions. The trade is a straightforward redistribution from the highest earners toward a broader, more adequate benefit, but the bill offers no path forward: it attracted only two cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: Hirono introduced it in July 2024, the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, and the committee never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on July 31, 2024, joined by Sens. Jeff Merkley and Tina Smith.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever taken, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners whose wages exceed the annual Social Security taxable cap are better off, because the additional payroll tax on income above the cap never took effect. The Social Security trust funds also gained nothing, so the projected financing shortfall was left unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who avoided the added tax

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley and Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote in the five months it had left in the session.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with no committee or floor action ever taken there was no record of any Republican position on the bill itself.

industries.industry: High-income wage earners and self-employed professionals
industries.note: The bill would phase out the exemption that stops Social Security payroll tax at the annual wage cap, meaning earners above it would pay tax on every additional dollar of wages from 2025 onward. They would receive only a tiny benefit credit (3 percent and 0.25 percent factors) on those earnings, so the extra tax is effectively a transfer to the broader program.

Employers owe the matching half of the Social Security payroll tax, so the bill would raise labor costs on wages above the cap for companies with well-paid staff. Ordinary workers earning below the cap would see no change in their own taxes.
